content.title: WHY YOUR 'HEALTHY' MEALS AREN'T ACTUALLY {{HEALTHY}}
facts: **Rice** – Skipping the rinse traps arsenic that clings to the starch coating, so a quick wash before boiling flushes a chunk of it away.
**Broccoli** – Boiling it to death drowns the enzyme myrosinase, the very thing that unlocks broccoli's sulforaphane; a quick steam keeps it alive and working.
**Turmeric** – Sprinkling it on without a pinch of black pepper or a splash of oil means most of the curcumin passes straight through you unused.
**Salmon** – Blasting it on high heat scorches the omega-3 fats, oxidizing them before they even hit your plate.
**Yogurt** – Stirring it into piping hot soup or oats kills off the live probiotic cultures you were counting on.
**Onions** – Cooking them the second they're chopped stops allicin from fully forming; a short rest first lets the compound develop.
**Lentils** – Skipping an overnight soak leaves more phytic acid behind, which can block your body from absorbing the minerals they carry.
**Quinoa** – A half-hearted rinse leaves bitter saponins behind that can upset a sensitive stomach.
**Tomatoes** – Eating them only raw shortchanges you; a few minutes of gentle cooking with a bit of oil releases more lycopene, not less.
**Sweet potatoes** – Peeling off the skin tosses out a big chunk of the fiber, wasting the part that keeps you full longest.
**Green tea** – Pouring boiling water straight over the leaves scalds the delicate catechins, weakening the antioxidant punch you're drinking it for.

content.caption:
Small kitchen habits quietly change what you're actually getting from your food. Take turmeric: on its own, curcumin is poorly absorbed, but the piperine in black pepper blocks the enzymes that break it down early, so pairing them can boost absorption dramatically. Broccoli works differently — its cancer-fighting sulforaphane only forms when the enzyme myrosinase meets its precursor compound, and high heat destroys that enzyme, which is why a light steam (or a sprinkle of raw broccoli sprouts after cooking) matters more than people think. And with rice, arsenic naturally accumulates from soil and water, so rinsing thoroughly and cooking it in extra water, then draining, meaningfully cuts down what ends up on your plate. Everyone's body and tolerance is different, so listen to yours.

This is exactly the kind of small detail we dig into at @smarthealthfix — from nutrition and common everyday symptoms to how your organs actually function and the tiny daily habits that quietly add up. Our mission is to help you build small, realistic habits instead of chasing quick fixes.
